newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end higher, but brokerages weak.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end higher, but brokerages weak.

text.p: Tokyo stocks ended higher on Monday as robust demand erased losses brought on by a report that a corporate racketeer told prosecutors that Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Daiwa Securities Co Ltd conducted illegal stock deals for him, brokers said.
The Nikkei 225 ended 81.21 points or 0.40 percent higher at 20,604.96. Its September futures ended flat at 20,570.
"Hopes that foreign investors would buy ahead of the June book closing eclipsed the brokerage losses caused by the report," said Paul Migliorato, senior sales person at Jardine Fleming Securities.

During the lunch break, Jiji news agency reported that the corporate racketeer at the centre of the Nomura Securities Co Ltd scandal had said that the "Big Four" brokerages had conducted illegal stock deals for him.
The Nikkei average fell to a low of 20,493.05 on the report while both Daiwa and Nikko slumped, due mainly to selling by short-term funds, brokers said.

Daiwa, the second most heavily traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo bourse with trade of 4.86 million shares, fell 45 yen to 904. Nikko ended 49 yen or 6.50 percent lower at 705, the third largest percentage loser.

Another domestic wire service later reported that another major brokerage, Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd, had also done illegal stock deals for the racketeer. Yamaichi ended down 10 at 341 yen. Daiwa, Nikko and Yamaichi spokesmen all declined to comment on the reports.

Brokers said that the report was not a bolt out of the blue as there had been rumors haunting the market of the possible involvement of other brokerages, limiting the losses to the sector and the brokerages themselves.
Securities was the top losing sector, followed by sea transport, land transport, mining and oil.

"If the reports are true, it will be a violation of the commercial code, but the impact of that alone is not enough to send the market reeling," said Mitsuru Hayashino, Sanyo Securities general manager.

"But the Nomura scandal has so far spread to Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd where a top former official has commited suicide and investors are keen to see how much further the scandal will widen," he added.
However, despite the anxiety over the scandal, brokers said that market direction was vague with investors quietly trading individual shares rather than sectors, thinning out trade.
Turnover totalled 317 million shares, down from 415 million on Friday. Winners nudged ahead of losers 541 to 533 while 189 issues were unchanged.

Participants are awaiting the policy-making U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting that starts on Tuesday and U.S. employment data due out on Thursday to see what they do to the U.S. stock market, brokers said.

"Most investors here don't think there will be a rate hike at the FOMC meeting, but they are curious about the reasons why there won't be a hike -- such as the outlook of the U.S. economy," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said.
Market sources speculated that Hong Kong's handover to China at Monday midnight would not have any immediate impact on the Tokyo stock market.
"But we'll watch where funds flow after the current bubble of Hong Kong stocks and real estate bursts," said Harushige Kobayashi, Yamaichi Securities deputy general manager.

NEC Corp tumbled 60 yen to 1,600 on a ratings cut by Nomura Securities. According to Nomura, NEC's investment in Packard Bell NEC (PB-NEC) was accumulating and there was a risk that the firm might not be able to recover its investment. NEC said Monday it would invest another $285 million in PB-NEC.
Nissan Motor Co Ltd, a car maker laggard, ended at a new high for calendar 1997, rising 29 yen to 889.
The gaining sectors were headed by air transport, gas, non-ferrous metals, rubber and automobiles.

The TOPIX index added 7.22 points or 0.47 percent to end at 1,553.81. The Nikkei 300 rose 1.92 points or 0.64 percent to 301.78. The second section index jumped 8.32 points or 0.45 percent to close at 1,848.25. Turnover was 8.46 million shares down slightly from 10.32 million on Friday.
-- Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-9052
